records.label: 4 1/2-year-old girl

phenotypes.text: short hair that had never been cut
abnormally shaped anagen bulbs lacking inner and outer root sheaths on trichogram
cleft formation between fragmented inner root sheaths and irregularly shaped hair shafts on scalp biopsy

quotes: We report on a 4 1/2-year-old girl affected by loose anagen hair and Noonan's syndrome.
The girl had short, blond, easily pluckable hair that had never been cut.
The trichogram showed an absolute prevalence of abnormally shaped anagen bulbs lacking inner and outer root sheaths.

records.label: 5-year-old boy with Noonan syndrome and loose anagen hair

phenotypes.text: predominance of anagen hairs devoid of sheaths on trichogram

quotes: Associated diseases included alopecia areata in a 3-year-old boy and Noonan syndrome in a 5-year-old boy.
In all cases, findings of a trichogram showed a predominance of anagen hairs (80% to 100%) devoid of sheaths.

records.label: Three children with Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair

phenotypes.text: mild dilatation of the pulmonary root

quotes: We present three children with short stature, the same facial phenotype, macrocephaly, enlarged cerebral spinal fluid spaces, short neck with redundant skin, severe GH deficiency, mild psychomotor delay with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), mild dilatation of the pulmonary root in two of them, and a unique combination of ectodermal abnormalities.
GH deficiency, darkly pigmented and hairless skin, and the unusual aspect of the hair, defined as loose anagen hair syndrome

records.label: 25 SHOC2 S2G mutation-positive subjects
records.segregation: De novo in 3 of 4 subjects of the first cohort and in 12 families of the second cohort where parental DNA was available; all cases sporadic
quotes: revealed an A-to-G transition at position 4 of the gene, predicting the Ser2Gly amino acid substitution (S2G), in four unrelated individuals
We observed 21 with the 4A>G missense change and proved that mutations were de novo in twelve families from which parental DNAs were available.

they exhibited reduced growth, which was frequently associated with proven GH deficiency, cognitive deficits, distinctive hyperactive behaviour that improved with age in most subjects, and hair anomalies including easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow growing hair

records.label: 8 SHOC2 p.S2G mutation-positive patients
quotes: We found the previously identified p.S2G mutation in eight of our patients.

All the patients with the p.S2G mutation showed short stature, sparse hair and atopic skin. Six of the mutation-positive patients showed severe mental retardation and easily pluckable hair, and one showed leukocytosis.

records.label: Male infant
quotes: The male infant presented with fetal distress requiring premature delivery at 32 weeks and was noted to have dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress following birth.
An echocardiogram revealed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.
detected the previously reported, pathogenic, de novo SHOC2 missense mutation predicting p.Ser2Gly

records.label: Patient 1 (CS# 229; LR13-109)

phenotypes.text: severe failure to thrive with gastrostomy tube

quotes: Postmortem testing of stored buccal cell derived DNA performed on a research basis revealed the recurrent SHOC2 c.4A>G mutation. This change was not present in either parent’s buccal cell derived DNA.
Bone marrow biopsies revealed markedly hypercellular marrow with crush artifacts suggestive of fibrosis and marked generalized increase in reticulin staining consistent with myelofibrosis.
He died at age 2 ½ years after splenectomy in preparation for a bone marrow transplant.

records.label: Patient 2 (CS#113; LR13-110)

phenotypes.text: severe feeding difficulties and failure to thrive

quotes: This male was the second child born to his 21-year-old mother and a 40-year-old father after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios.
Macrocephaly, unilateral ptosis, posteriorly angulated ears, increased wrinkling of the palms, loose skin, bilateral inguinal hernias and hypotonia were noted, and Costello syndrome was considered.
SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly | +, de novo | +, de novo | + | + | + | + | +

records.label: Patient 3 (CS#134)

phenotypes.text: increased palmar wrinkling and deep palmar creases

quotes: He had right bundle branch block, and mild to moderate biventricular hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) at age 6 months.
He was diagnosed with pervasive developmental disorder and Tourette syndrome at 9 years and continued to use psychotropic medications.
His height was 125 cm (10th centile), weight 29.4 kg (50th centile) and OFC 60 cm (+5 SD) at age 9 years.

records.label: Patient 4 (LR#12-389)

phenotypes.text: sparse, thin, easily pluckable blond hair
absent transverse sinuses / abnormal venous anatomy

quotes: This male was born to a 32-year-old G2P1-2 mother and a 41-year-old father of Mexican ancestry at 37 weeks gestation with a weight of 2.9 kg (50–75th centile).

A brain MRI revealed mild ventriculomegaly and subependymal heterotopia (Fig. 2). Subsequent brain and spinal MRIs performed at 6 years due to headaches revealed development of a Chiari 1 malformation (Table II) in the context of platybasia and basilar invagination, and segmental fusion of the C3 and C4 vertebrae.
Patient 4 was referred after molecular diagnosis of a SHOC2 mutation

records.label: Patient 5 (LR#12-454)

phenotypes.text: relatively small cerebellar vermis and hemispheres
wide chest with mild pectus excavatum
abnormal mitral valve with three papillary muscles

quotes: His neonatal course was complicated by hypotonia and feeding difficulties, resulting in naso-gastric feeding tube use until about age 1 year.

A brain MRI at age 3 weeks (Fig. 3) showed a relatively small cerebellar vermis and hemispheres with prominent fluid spaces above and below the cerebellum, and increased extra-axial fluid spaces over the frontal lobes and sylvian fissures.
Echocardiography showed an abnormal mitral valve with three papillary muscles and redundant mitral valve chordae.

records.label: Proband (5-year-old female)

phenotypes.text: irregularities in midbrain, pons and medulla on MRI

records.segregation: Inherited from father, who also had mild features
quotes: The first patient is a 5 year old female referred for evaluation of right optic nerve hypoplasia, bilateral nystagmus, speech delay, poor hair growth and hyperactive behavior.

She had average stature (47th percentile), macrocephaly (98th percentile), sparse and slow-growing hair which was not loose, normal skin pigmentation, bilateral ptosis and nystagmus, normal chest with wide-spaced nipples, and clubbed nails (Fig. 1A and B).
She does not have short stature, a cardiac anomaly, hyperpigmentation, ichthyosis or loose anagen hair.
records.genotype_reason: single heterozygous variant; mode as stated for the family

records.label: Proband's father
quotes: Both parents were tested, and our proband’s father had a heterozygous copy of the p.M173I variant. He was 6′3″ tall, had intellectual disability, a high-arched palate, sparse hair and clubbed nails (Fig. 1C, D, and E).
Echocardiograms and renal ultrasounds on both patients were negative
records.genotype_reason: single heterozygous variant; mode as stated for the family

records.label: Patient with SHOC2 p.Gln269_His270delinsHisTyr
quotes: Here, we report on the third RASopathy-causing SHOC2 mutation (c.807_808delinsTT, p.Gln269_His270delinsHisTyr), which was found associated with prenatal-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

notes.statement: Motta et al. (2019) found that the SHOC2 c.807_808delinsTT (p.Gln269_His270delinsHisTyr) mutation was activating: the mutant protein showed enhanced binding to MRAS and PPP1CB and increased signaling through the MAPK cascade. Structural analyses suggested a possible effect on the relative orientation of the two leucine-rich repeat domains of SHOC2.
quotes: Structural analyses indicated a possible impact of the mutation on the relative orientation of the two SHOC2's leucine-rich repeat domains.
Functional studies provided evidence of its activating role, revealing enhanced binding of the mutant protein to MRAS and PPP1CB, and increased signaling through the MAPK cascade.

notes.statement: Motta et al. (2019) showed that, unlike the recurrent S2G mutant, SHOC2 Q269_H270delinsHY was not constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane, and concluded that diverse mechanisms of SHOC2 functional dysregulation converge toward upregulation of MAPK signaling.
quotes: Differing from SHOC2 S2G , SHOC2 Q269_H270delinsHY is not constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane.
These data document that diverse mechanisms in SHOC2 functional dysregulation converge toward MAPK signaling upregulation.

notes.statement: Young et al. (2018) found that MRAS interacts with SHOC2 and protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) to form a heterotrimeric holoenzyme. This holoenzyme dephosphorylates the inhibitory S259 site of RAF kinases (S259 on CRAF, S365 on BRAF). MRAS and SHOC2 act as PP1 regulatory subunits that make the complex highly specific for RAF, and MRAS membrane localization is needed for efficient RAF dephosphorylation and ERK pathway regulation.
quotes: The MRAS GTPase, a close relative of RAS oncoproteins, interacts with SHOC2 and protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) to form a heterotrimeric holoenzyme that dephosphorylates this S259 RAF site.
MRAS and SHOC2 function as PP1 regulatory subunits providing the complex with striking specificity against RAF.
MRAS also functions as a targeting subunit as membrane localization is required for efficient RAF dephosphorylation and ERK pathway regulation in cells.

notes.statement: Young et al. (2018) noted that the predicted structure of SHOC2 closely resembles the A subunit of PP2A, which suggests convergent structural evolution with the PP2A heterotrimer. They identified several regions in SHOC2 involved in complex formation, as well as residues in MRAS switch I and the interswitch region that help explain why MRAS specifically binds SHOC2-PP1.
quotes: SHOC2's predicted structure shows remarkable similarities to the A subunit of PP2A, suggesting a case of convergent structural evolution with the PP2A heterotrimer.

We have identified multiple regions in SHOC2 involved in complex formation as well as residues in MRAS switch I and the interswitch region that help account for MRAS's unique effector specificity for SHOC2-PP1.

notes.statement: Young et al. (2018) showed that Noonan syndrome mutations in SHOC2, MRAS and PPP1CB all promoted formation of the complex among these three proteins, but did not necessarily increase binding to other interactors. They concluded that Noonan syndrome in individuals with SHOC2, MRAS or PPP1CB mutations is likely driven at the biochemical level by enhanced ternary complex formation.
quotes: MRAS, SHOC2, and PPP1CB are mutated in Noonan syndrome, and we show that syndromic mutations invariably promote complex formation with each other, but not necessarily with other interactors.
Thus, Noonan syndrome in individuals with SHOC2, MRAS, or PPPC1B mutations is likely driven at the biochemical level by enhanced ternary complex formation

notes.statement: Bertola et al. (2017) reported a 12-year-old Brazilian boy with the recurrent p.Pro49Arg mutation in PPP1CB. He had sparse, thin, slow-growing hair similar to that seen in Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair, and he also had craniosynostosis. The authors concluded that PPP1CB-related Noonan syndrome with loose anagen hair is very similar to Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair.
quotes: We report on a 12-year-old Brazilian boy with the p.Pro49Arg mutation in PPP1CB, a novel gene associated with RASopathies.
Phenotypically, he also showed the same hair pattern-sparse, thin, and with slow growing-, similar to the typical ectodermal finding observed in Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair.
This report gives further support that this novel RASopathy-PPP1CB-related Noonan syndrome with loose anagen hair-shares great similarity to Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair

notes.statement: Hannig et al. (2014) found that the SHOC2 M173I variant restored EGF-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation only about 10% above the basal level in SHOC2-depleted Cos1 cells, whereas wildtype SHOC2 rescued it fully. The variant did not affect protein half-life, subcellular localization or binding to M-RAS and RAF-1.
quotes: the SHOC2 (M173I)-tRFP mutant expressed to a similar level as WT SHOC2-tRFP was only able to restore ~10% above the basal level of EGF-induced ERK1/2 activity
The capacity of SHOC2-M173I to form a complex with M-RAS and RAF-1 was comparable to that of WT SHOC2 (Fig. 2C)

notes.statement: Hannig et al. (2014) found that the M173I mutant of SHOC2 failed to precipitate endogenous PP1c effectively and supported only a mild increase in RAF-1 Ser338 phosphorylation after EGF stimulation. They concluded that reduced binding of SHOC2 to PP1c caused the ERK1/2 pathway dysregulation, making the variant loss-of-function.
quotes: the GST-tagged M173I mutant of SHOC2 failed to precipitate endogenous PP1c effectively, suggesting that the M173I substitution alters the interaction of SHOC2 and PP1c.

Our data show that p.M173I is a functional variant by demonstrating that it causes an alteration in ERK1/2 activity and that reduced binding of SHOC2 to the catalytic subunit of PP1c is the cause of the ERK1/2 pathway dysregulation.
The p.M173I SHOC2 substitution causes loss of function in the ERK1/2 pathway.

notes.statement: Hannig et al. (2014) noted that the phenotype of patients with the SHOC2 M173I variant differed significantly from that of patients with the S2G mutation. These patients lacked short stature, cardiac anomalies and loose anagen hair. The authors concluded that SHOC2 mutations can cause a spectrum of Rasopathy phenotypes of varying severity.
quotes: Phenotypic features of patients with the M173I mutation are significantly different from those reported for patients with the c.4A>G; p.S2G SHOC2 mutation.
We thus conclude that SHOC2 mutations can cause a spectrum of Rasopathy phenotypes of varying severity.

notes.statement: Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 patients with the SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly mutation. All had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse light-colored hair, increased fine wrinkles, ligamentous laxity, and developmental delay, and all 4 with available data had a structural cardiac anomaly. Brain imaging showed relative megalencephaly, enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, and a small posterior fossa with a vertical tentorium.
quotes: All had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse light colored hair, increased fine wrinkles, ligamentous laxity, developmental delay, and 4/4 had a structural cardiac anomaly.

Distinctive brain abnormalities included relative megalencephaly and enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, and a relatively small posterior fossa as indicated by a vertical tentorium.

notes.statement: Gripp et al. (2013) noted that 4 of the 5 patients had initially been suspected of having Costello syndrome. They found that the patients' light-colored, slow-growing scalp hair with dolichocilia resembled the hair seen in Costello syndrome caused by HRAS p.Gly13Cys. The authors said this supports testing patients with a RASopathy phenotype using a gene panel.
quotes: This combination of light colored, slow growing and unruly textured scalp hair with dolichocilia (extremely long eye lashes) is typical for Costello syndrome resulting from an uncommon HRAS change, p.Gly13Cys.

One might thus anticipate that, like Patients 1, 2, 3 and 5, additional individuals with a suspected diagnosis of Costello syndrome will have the SHOC2 mutation, supporting the use of a panel approach to molecular testing in patients with a rasopathy phenotype.

notes.statement: Gripp et al. (2013) found Chiari 1 malformation in 3 of 8 SHOC2 mutation-positive patients with MRI data, including their own and previously reported patients. They attributed it to the combination of relative megalencephaly with a small posterior fossa, and noted that it can develop after birth.
quotes: Adding the patient in whom a MRI obtained at age 9 years revealed a Chiari 1 malformation, 3/8 patients in whom MRIs were obtained had a Chiari 1.
The combination of relative megalencephaly and small posterior fossa likely resulted in Patient 4’s postnatal development of a Chiari I malformation.

notes.statement: Gripp et al. (2013) reported the first hematologic neoplasm in a patient with a SHOC2 mutation: myelofibrosis in a 2-year-old. Because the patient lacked the JAK2 p.Val617Phe mutation, the authors suggested that the SHOC2 mutation may have predisposed to myelofibrosis through activation of the Ras/MAPK pathway. They proposed testing JAK2-negative myelofibrosis cases for SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly.
quotes: The absence of the common JAK2 mutation in Patient 1 is noteworthy and suggests that the SHOC2 mutation may have been the predisposing change for myelofibrosis.
We suggest to study JAK2 mutation negative myelofibrosis cases for SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly.

notes.statement: Pooling 2 earlier case series, Gripp et al. (2013) estimated that SHOC2 mutations occur in about 6% (12 of 188) of patients with Noonan syndrome who lack a mutation in other known genes. They calculated that this corresponds to about 1.8% of all individuals with Noonan syndrome.
quotes: Assuming no overlap between these case series, the incidence of a SHOC2 mutation is 12/188, or about 6%. However, at least 70% of all Noonan syndrome patients have a mutation in a previously reported gene; thus 6% of the remaining 30% would reflect 1.8% of all individuals with Noonan syndrome.

notes.statement: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a premature male infant with the de novo SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly mutation whose hypertrophic cardiomyopathy progressed rapidly, leading to discharge for palliative care. They noted that his cardiac findings and other features were not typical of patients previously reported with this mutation, and concluded that the case expanded the clinical phenotype.
quotes: The infant's cardiac lesion rapidly progressed, and he was discharged home for palliative care.
The patient's cardiac findings and features were not typical for those individuals previously reported with this SHOC2 mutation and thus expand the clinical phenotype.

notes.statement: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) analyzed SHOC2 in 92 patients with Noonan syndrome and related disorders who did not have mutations in PTPN11, KRAS, HRAS, BRAF, MAP2K1/2, SOS1 or RAF1. They found the previously identified p.S2G mutation in 8 of these patients.
quotes: we analyzed SHOC2 in 92 patients with Noonan syndrome and related disorders who did not exhibit PTPN11, KRAS, HRAS, BRAF, MAP2K1/2, SOS1 or RAF1 mutations. We found the previously identified p.S2G mutation in eight of our patients.

notes.statement: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) developed a rapid melting curve analysis method to detect the SHOC2 p.S2G mutation. They proposed it as a useful tool for screening for this apparently common mutation.
quotes: We developed a rapid detection system to identify the p.S2G mutation using melting curve analysis, which will be a useful tool to screen for the apparently common mutation.

notes.statement: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) found no SHOC2 mutations in leukemia cells from 82 patients with leukemia.
quotes: No SHOC2 mutations were identified in leukemia cells from 82 leukemia patients.

notes.statement: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) concluded that the clinical features of SHOC2 mutation-positive patients partly overlap with those of typical Noonan or CFC syndrome. They also concluded that easily pluckable/loose anagen hair is distinctive in these patients.
quotes: These results suggest that clinical manifestations in SHOC2 mutation-positive patients partially overlap with those in patients with typical Noonan or CFC syndrome and show that easily pluckable/loose anagen hair is distinctive in SHOC2 mutation-positive patients.

notes.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) identified SHOC2 as a candidate by in silico protein network analysis and found the 4A>G (S2G) change in 4 of 96 mutation-negative Noonan syndrome patients and 21 of 410 further mutation-negative subjects with NS or related phenotypes. No other disease-associated SHOC2 variant was found, suggesting a specific pathogenetic role for S2G.
quotes: We then analyzed SHOC2 in a cohort of 410 mutation-negative subjects with NS or a related phenotype.
No additional disease-associated SHOC2 sequence variant was identified in the analyzed cohort, strongly suggesting a specific pathogenetic role for the S2G amino acid substitution.

notes.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) noted that referring pediatricians felt several of the SHOC2-mutation-positive subjects had features suggestive of Costello or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome as newborns or young infants, and that mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects were overrepresented compared with the general NS population.
quotes: Of note, the referring pediatricians felt that several of these subjects had features suggestive of Costello syndrome or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome, as newborns or young infants.
Cardiac anomalies were observed in the majority of the cases, with dysplasia of the mitral valve and septal defects significantly overrepresented compared with the general NS population.

notes.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) showed that the S2G substitution created an N-myristoylation site: SHOC2(S2G) incorporated [3H]-myristic acid whereas wildtype and S2A did not, and the mutant was constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane and failed to translocate to the nucleus upon EGF stimulation. Membrane localization was reduced by the NMT inhibitor 2-hydroxymyristic acid.
quotes: SHOC2S2G incorporated [3H]-myristic acid, while the wild type protein and the disease-unrelated SHOC2S2A did not.
In contrast, SHOC2S2G was specifically targeted to the cell membrane in both states.
Treatment with 2-hydroxymyristic acid, an NMT inhibitor, at varying doses reduced or abolished SHOC2S2G’s membrane localization

notes.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that SHOC2(S2G) did not heterodimerize with wildtype SHOC2, excluding a dominant-negative effect, and that its expression enhanced EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation in Neuro2A cells but not in Cos-1 or 293T cells, indicating cell type-specific MAPK activation.
quotes: The experiments demonstrated that these proteins do not heterodimerize, ruling out that possibility.
SHOC2S2G expression promoted enhanced EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation compared to wild type SHOC2, in neuroblastoma Neuro2A cells

notes.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that wildtype SHOC2 was distributed in the cytoplasm and nucleus in starved cells and was restricted to the nucleus after EGF stimulation; growth factor-stimulated nuclear translocation of endogenous SHOC2 was confirmed in primary skin fibroblasts.
quotes: SHOC2wt was uniformly distributed in the cytoplasm and nucleus in starved cells but was restricted to the nucleus following EGF stimulation
Growth factor-stimulated nuclear translocation of the endogenous SHOC2 protein was confirmed in primary skin fibroblasts (Fig. 2e).

notes.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that in C. elegans, human SHOC2 wildtype but not S2G rescued sur-8 function. Expression of SHOC2(S2G) or myristoylation-tagged wildtype SHOC2 at early L3 caused protruding vulva, egg-laying defects and a bag-of-worms phenotype through abnormal vulval morphogenesis, without altering vulval cell fate specification.
quotes: While SHOC2wt was able to replace SUR-8 functionally, SHOC2S2G failed to do so.

at early L3 stage, it caused abnormal vulval development, resulting in protruding vulva (Pvl), decreased egg laying efficiency (Egl) and accumulation of larvae inside the mother with the formation of bag-of-worms adults (Bag phenotype)
These neomorphic phenotypes were absent in animals expressing SHOC2wt but were also observed when SHOC2wt tagged with an N-myristoylation sequence (myr::SHOC2wt) was expressed

notes.statement: Mazzanti et al. (2003) proposed that the combination of a facial appearance not completely typical of Noonan syndrome, a behavioral phenotype, GH deficiency, darkly pigmented hairless skin, and loose anagen hair represented a distinct, previously unreported syndrome, which they named 'Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair.'
quotes: Their appearance, not completely typical of Noonan syndrome, the behavioral phenotype, GH deficiency, darkly pigmented and hairless skin, and the unusual aspect of the hair, defined as loose anagen hair syndrome did not fit any known condition.
We postulate that these children may represent a distinct, previously unreported syndrome that we would name "Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair".

notes.statement: Tosti et al. (1997) reviewed 19 patients diagnosed with loose anagen hair (14 children and 5 adults). Associated conditions included Noonan syndrome in a 5-year-old boy. The authors concluded that loose anagen hair may be sporadic, may occur together with developmental or acquired conditions, or, less commonly, may be familial.
quotes: Beginning in January 1990, 14 children and 5 adults (age range, 8 months to 47 years) were diagnosed as having LAH. Associated diseases included alopecia areata in a 3-year-old boy and Noonan syndrome in a 5-year-old boy.
The development of LAH may be sporadic, occur in association with developmental or acquired conditions, or, less commonly, be a familial disorder.

notes.statement: In all patients with loose anagen hair studied by Tosti et al. (1997), the trichogram showed mostly anagen hairs (80 to 100%) lacking sheaths. Pathologic study of hair from 5 patients found no morphologic abnormalities of the hair follicles apart from frequent fragmentation of the inner root sheath. The authors concluded that pathology is of little diagnostic value.
quotes: In all cases, findings of a trichogram showed a predominance of anagen hairs (80% to 100%) devoid of sheaths.
The pathologic study of hair from 5 patients did not reveal morphological abnormalities of the hair follicles except for a high incidence of fragmentations of the inner root sheath.
The pathologic findings of LAH do not demonstrate any specific features and are of little value in the diagnosis of this condition.
